title: Timed mock habits in Python (floor division, deque, recursion limits)
seriesDescription: Shortest paths, union-find, tries, intervals, bits, dynamic programming, greedy and backtracking with Python code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Python-specific habits for the 25-minute round: floor division, identity versus equality, deque versus list.pop(0), recursion depth and edge-case tests.
source: Python docs (data model, collections.deque, sys.setrecursionlimit, round); Fluent Python (Ramalho); Tech Interview Handbook

questions.prompt: What does -7 // 2 evaluate to in Python?
questions.explanation: // is floor division: -7 / 2 = -3.5 rounds down to -4, not toward zero. The remainder follows: -7 % 2 is 1. Use int(-7 / 2) if you need truncation toward zero (-3).

questions.prompt: In Python, what does 10**5 * 10**5 evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Python ints are arbitrary precision, so the product is exactly 10,000,000,000 with no overflow. The cost is speed, which is why n * n for n = 10^5 is still too slow as a loop count, even though it is a valid number.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function lower_bound(a, target) that returns the first index i with a[i] >= target in a sorted list (len(a) if none), using a loop and a half-open range, without the bisect module.
questions.explanation: Python ints never overflow, so (lo + hi) // 2 is safe, unlike in fixed-width languages. In real code bisect.bisect_left does exactly this. The half-open range makes lo the answer with no fix-ups at the end.

checks.label: computes the midpoint with integer division
moves lo or hi depending on a[mid] < target

questions.prompt: In Python, write three assert statements for merge(intervals) (which returns a list of [start, end] lists): an empty input, touching intervals [1,2] and [2,3], and a nested pair [1,10] and [2,3].
questions.explanation: Pick expected values you can verify by hand. Input order matters in the touching case: [2,3] first would test the sort as well. Frameworks like pytest.mark.parametrize group these, but plain asserts are fine in an interview.

questions.prompt: True or false: using `is` to compare two integers, as in a is b, is a reliable way to test that they are equal.
questions.explanation: Small ints are cached by CPython as an implementation detail, so `is` can appear to work in tests and then fail on bigger values.

options.why: `is` tests object identity; equal large ints may be different objects, so the result can vary.
Correct: use == for values and reserve is for None and other singletons.

questions.prompt: You need a FIFO queue for BFS in a Python interview solution. Which choice is the idiomatic one?
questions.explanation: Use deque for BFS and sliding windows; reserve queue.Queue for producer and consumer threads.

options.why: Correct: both ends are O(1) and it needs no lock.

options.text: A list, using pop(0), because it is the simplest container.
options.why: pop(0) shifts every remaining item, so each dequeue is O(n).

options.text: queue.Queue, because it is the standard queue class.
options.why: It is built for thread communication and adds locking overhead.

options.text: heapq, because a heap always returns the oldest item first.
options.why: A heap returns the smallest item, not the oldest.

questions.prompt: A recursive DFS on a path-shaped graph of 100,000 nodes raises RecursionError. What is the best response in an interview?
questions.explanation: Raising sys.setrecursionlimit is a quick patch but can crash the interpreter on very deep recursion; say both and prefer the explicit stack.

options.text: Rewrite it with an explicit stack, which has no call-depth limit.
options.why: Correct: the iterative form needs only heap memory.

options.text: Catch RecursionError and return the partial result computed so far.
options.why: A partial result is a wrong answer for most graph problems.

options.text: Convert the adjacency lists to a dict, which recurses less deeply.
options.why: The container type has no effect on call depth.

options.text: Add lru_cache so each node is visited only once and the depth shrinks.
options.why: Caching avoids repeated work but does not reduce the depth of a single chain.

questions.prompt: A Python function returns the maximum subarray sum of a list. Select all that apply: which inputs belong in your own tests?
questions.explanation: Also try an empty list (agree on the expected behaviour) and alternating signs.

options.text: A list with a single element.
options.why: Correct: it checks initialisation of the running best.

options.text: Only the sample from the problem statement.
options.why: The sample rarely exercises initialisation or signs.

options.text: A list where every element is negative.
options.why: Correct: starting the best at 0 would wrongly return 0.

options.text: A list containing zeros and repeated values.
options.why: Correct: they probe the strictness of comparisons.

options.text: A dictionary, since Python functions accept any type.
options.why: The contract says list; testing other types is outside the spec.

questions.prompt: Match each Python trouble spot in a timed round with the habit that avoids it.
questions.explanation: Each habit is a one-line fix you can say aloud: it shows the interviewer you know where Python bites.

left.text: Building a string with += in a loop
A mutable default argument like path=[]
Deep recursion hits the call limit

right.text: Default to None and create the list inside
Use an explicit stack or iterate
Build rows with a list comprehension

questions.prompt: Complete the Python habits for a timed round.
questions.explanation: ''.join avoids quadratic copying, deque gives O(1) popleft, and floor division rounds toward negative infinity (-7 // 2 is -4).
questions.text: Use {1} to build a string from pieces, a {2} for a queue, and remember that // rounds toward {3}.

questions.prompt: Using a Python list as a BFS queue.
questions.assertion: list.pop(0) takes O(n) time, so it is a poor queue for large inputs.
questions.reason: Removing the first item shifts every remaining item one position to the left.

whys.a: Right: the shift is exactly why each pop(0) is linear.
whys.b: R is the direct cause of A.

questions.explanation: Stability lets you sort by a secondary key first and a primary key second.
questions.assertion: sorted(items, key=f) is a stable sort.
questions.reason: sorted returns a new list and leaves the original unchanged.

whys.a: Returning a new list does not explain stability; the Timsort algorithm does.
whys.b: Right: both are true, but they are independent properties.

questions.explanation: most_common(k) sorts, so it costs O(n log n) in the worst case, or O(n log k) with a heap.
questions.assertion: Counter(s) counts the occurrences of every character of s in O(n) time.
questions.reason: Counter always keeps its keys sorted by count.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: A is true, but Counter keeps insertion order; only most_common() sorts by count, so R is false.

questions.explanation: For half-up rounding use int(x + 0.5) for non-negative x, or the decimal module.
questions.reason: Python rounds halves to the nearest even number.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.d: Right: R is true and is why A is false; round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4.
